newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-CONTRASTING FORTUNES AHEAD OF SEVILLE DERBY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CONTRASTING FORTUNES AHEAD OF SEVILLE DERBY.

text.p: Local rivals Sevilla and Real Betis could hardly go into this Sunday's big game in the Spanish first division with more contrasting fortunes.
Whereas Real Betis are riding high in fourth, Sevilla are third from bottom in a season when four teams will face automatic relegation.
It's a dramatic turn-around after years when Sevilla were challenging for a UEFA Cup place while their neighbours were languishing in the second division.
And Sevilla's problems aren't confined to the pitch.
A series of humilliating financial scandals have left fans baying for the blood of Jose Maria Gonzalez, Sevilla's fourth president in less than eighteen months.
The problems at the club -- which in the 65,000-capacity Sanchez Pizjuan stadium has Spain's third-biggest ground -- date from the summer of 1995.

After qualifying for European competition, Sevilla players had their holidays interrupted by the news that the team had been relegated to the third division after breaking league accountancy regulations.
Sevilla were eventually reprieved, but the shock clearly played a role in the club's worst season in years.
Jose Antonio Camacho, a man widely tipped as a future Real Madrid manager, was signed from Espanyol to put things right.
But Camacho found that the club was unable to finance the signings he wanted, and an atmosphere of incompetence surrounded the transfers that were squeezed out of the management.
Forgeries were discovered in documents relating to the purchase of Argentine midfielder Christian Colusso, while Sevilla paid Barcelona for Robert Prosinecki with blank cheques.
There has even been speculation that Brazilian World Cup striker Bebeto will return to Flamengo because of non-payment of his transfer fee.
